title: The Effects of Imagery and Self-Talk on Bouldering Performance
abstract: Abstract: Olympic bouldering combines high physical demands with complex cognitive and psychological requirements, making both physical and psychological performance factors relevant for success. While most studies on bouldering performance have investigated the role of several physiological determinants, research on psychological aspects remains limited. Imagery and self-talk (ST) are two well-established psychological techniques recommended for optimizing performance in several sports, yet there is limited empirical evidence investigating their effectiveness in bouldering. The aim of this study was to examine the effects of a PETTLEP imagery intervention and ST on bouldering performance, and to determine whether imagery ability moderates the effects of the imagery intervention on performance. In total, 58 experienced climbers ( n = 17 female, M age = 31.47, SD age = 9.26) were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: an imagery condition using PETTLEP imagery, an ST condition practicing motivational and positive ST, or a non-treatment control condition (CC). Performance was measured by the number of completed moves (bouldering points, BPs) and bouldering time (BT) on a Kilter Board. Imagery ability was assessed using the Vividness of Movement Imagery Questionnaire-2 (VMIQ-2) and mental chronometry. Results from a mixed ANOVA revealed that the imagery condition significantly increased BPs on the Kilter Board from the first to the second measurement time, whereas no significant improvements were observed in the ST condition or CC. No significant effects were found regarding changes in BT. Multiple regression analyses showed that mental chronometry scores predicted improvements in BPs after the imagery intervention, and both the mental chronometry and VMIQ-2 scores predicted changes in BT. In summary, the findings provide preliminary evidence that PETTLEP imagery may have the potential to enhance bouldering performance, particularly among climbers with higher imagery ability.
